analysis.one_liner: Banned the nerve-agent pesticide chlorpyrifos from all food grown in the United States.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it died in the Senate Agriculture Committee when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Chlorpyrifos is a pesticide originally developed as a World War II nerve agent. EPA's own 2016 assessment found that food and drinking-water exposures exceed the agency's safety standard — children ages 1 to 2 were estimated to be exposed to 140 times the acceptable level — and that farmworkers are exposed to unsafe levels even with full protective gear. The bill would have banned any food containing chlorpyrifos, ordered an independent National Research Council review of the whole organophosphate class, and required EPA to act within 90 days whenever it finds unsafe exposure to any organophosphate pesticide.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, whose developing brains are most vulnerable to prenatal and early-life exposure; farmworkers and their families, who face the heaviest exposures from mixing, spraying, and re-entering sprayed fields; and people in agricultural communities whose drinking water and air are contaminated by spray drift.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the sale of any food containing chlorpyrifos or its breakdown products, ending dietary exposure to a pesticide EPA found exceeds its safety standard for children.

Requires EPA to contract with the National Research Council for an independent risk assessment of all organophosphate pesticides, covering infants, children, fetuses, and agricultural workers, and aggregating diet, drift, workplace, and take-home exposure routes.

Requires EPA to take regulatory action within 90 days of learning of any organophosphate exposure that fails federal safety standards, replacing the open-ended timeline that had left EPA's own 2015 proposed ban unresolved.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of chlorpyrifos lose a major product line, and growers of apples, broccoli, almonds, walnuts, onions, cauliflower, corn, and other crops lose a widely used insect-control tool and would bear the cost of switching to alternatives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers and farmers who spray it

drawbacks.text: Chlorpyrifos was applied to more than 50 percent of the nation's apple and broccoli crops and to large shares of onion, walnut, and cauliflower acreage, so growers losing it would face higher pest-control costs and may lack equally effective substitutes, costs that could be passed to consumers.

The bill writes a single chemical's ban directly into law and sets a hard 90-day deadline for EPA action on any organophosphate, which critics would call an end-run around the normal scientific review process — even though the bill relies on the EPA record already developed.
Alternatives to chlorpyrifos carry their own costs and risks, and a phase-out without transition support lands hardest on growers with the thinnest margins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health side is strongly documented in the government's own record: EPA found no acceptable uses, all food uses exceed the safety standard, children's exposures reached 140 times acceptable levels, and farmworkers are poisoned even with maximum protective equipment. Against that, growers lose an effective and inexpensive tool and would face real transition costs. On balance the health benefits to children and farmworkers outweigh the costs to agriculture, and the bill's reliance on EPA's existing science rather than new assertions keeps it within the ordinary regulatory framework.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 10 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, never taken up, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the bill on July 25, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
The bill attracted 10 Senate Democratic cosponsors but no Republicans.
The committee took no further action — no hearing markup or vote is recorded — and the bill expired at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

The bill was a response to EPA's own finding in November 2016 that chlorpyrifos residues and drinking-water exposures exceed the legal safety standard; the bill would have converted that finding into a statutory ban rather than waiting on EPA.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chlorpyrifos manufacturers and the growers who kept spraying it came out ahead; children, farmworkers, and rural residents kept absorbing the exposure EPA had already found to be unsafe. Months after introduction, the Trump EPA withdrew the proposed ban and kept the pesticide legal, a decision widely reported as following chemical-industry pressure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide makers and growers who kept using it

for.name: Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban chlorpyrifos on food and force a review of all organophosphate pesticides.

for.name: 10 of 46 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Blumenthal, Booker, Durbin, Gillibrand, Markey, Harris, Cardin, and Merkley.

against.name: Pat Roberts
against.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee never took up the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

against.name: Trump EPA (Administrator Scott Pruitt)
against.what_they_did: In March 2017, reversed EPA's 2015 proposal to ban chlorpyrifos on food, keeping the pesticide legal and removing the agency action the bill was designed to force.

against.name: Chlorpyrifos manufacturers and user industries
against.role: Pesticide producers and agricultural chemical interests
against.what_they_did: Opposed revoking chlorpyrifos tolerances and pressed EPA and Congress to keep the pesticide registered.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the Republican-controlled Agriculture Committee took no action, and no vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated food uses of one of the most widely applied organophosphate insecticides, a product whose legal status depends on overriding EPA's own finding that its uses fail the safety standard. Keeping it registered preserved manufacturer revenue at the cost of exposures to children and farmworkers.

industries.industry: Fruit, vegetable, and nut growers using chlorpyrifos
industries.note: Growers of apples, broccoli, onions, walnuts, and cauliflower relied on chlorpyrifos on 40 to 50 percent of those crops and would have borne the cost of switching to other controls. Their interest in keeping the cheaper chemical runs against the public's interest in residue-free food and uncontaminated drinking water.

industries.industry: Producers of alternative insecticides and organic growers
industries.note: A chlorpyrifos ban would shift demand toward competing insect-control products and growers already operating without organophosphates.
